Five of the 12 patients were managed with chemotherapy. Eight
patients were reported to die of progressive disease.
Angiosarcomas can be difﬁcult to remove completely because of
their inﬁltrative nature, vascularity and propensity to metastasize.
Several reports describe surgery as the mainstay of treatment and
recommend radiotherapy alone for treating surgically inaccessible
tumors.2,9 Successful en bloc spondylectomy of a spinal angiosar-
coma has been reported. 3 This technique is based on sound onco-
logical principles and aims to completely resection the tumor
with clear histological margins. Some patients with angiosarcoma
are not candidates for en bloc spondylectomy due to extensive epi-
dural disease, multilevel vertebral body involvement, and large
paraspinal masses, as in our patient.
Of the 13 reported patients, one died of complications related to
medullary compression from extradural hematoma,
10 one patient
experienced progressive upper-extremity radiculopathy with
weakness due to epidural hematoma, 11 and three had excessive
intraoperative bleeding. 9,11,12 Preoperative embolization may re-
duce bleeding during resection. Additionally, preoperative emboli-
zation ensures an unimpeded view of the surgical ﬁeld and may
shrink the tumor, increasing the likelihood of achieving complete
tumor resection. Angiography is also important for deﬁning the
vascular anatomy of large tumors.
4. Conclusion
We report the ﬁrst patient with a spinal angiosarcoma arising
from the posterior elements without vertebral body destruction.
Successful treatment required selective angiography and emboli-
zation, combined with radical tumor excision. Because these tu-
mors occur infrequently, documentation of the long-term
outcomes of tumor operations is important. Additional patient re-
ports are needed for further insight into their clinical course and
outcome.
Appendix A. Supplementary data
Supplementary data associated with this article can be found, in
the online version, at doi:10.1016/j.jocn.2009.03.049.

Rituximab treatment of stiff-person syndrome in a patient with thymoma,
diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroiditis
J.L. Dupond *, L. Essalmi, H. Gil, N. Meaux-Ruault, C. Hafsaoui
Department of Internal Medicine, University Hospital, Boulevard Fleming, Besançon 25030, France
article info
Article history:
Received 3 March 2009
Accepted 10 June 2009
Keywords:
Stiff-person syndrome
Anti-amphiphysin antibodies
Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies
Thymoma
Rituximab
abstract
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune neurological disorder characterized by stiffness of the
skeletal muscle with superimposed spasms and production of autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase (GAD) and amphiphysin. The disorder results from B cell-mediated clonal production of autoanti-
bodies, requiring treatment with immunosuppressors; however, treatment results have been
somewhat inconsistent. We report the results of rituximab treatment in a patient with SPS associated
with a thymoma, diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroiditis and the presence of anti-GAD and anti-
amphiphysin autoantibodies. The patient experienced a partial improvement following a thymectomy
and the administration of prednisone, intravenous immunoglobulins and mycophenolate mofetil. Treat-
ment with rituximab was followed by a complete sustained remission and the disappearance of serum
anti-amphiphysin antibodies.

1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurological disorder char-
acterized by progressive muscle rigidity with superimposed pain-
ful muscle spasms and gait impairment, owing to continuous
motor activity. SPS is an autoimmune, predominantly encephal-
omyelopathic disorder resulting from B cell-mediated clonal pro-
duction of autoantibodies against presynaptic inhibitory epitopes
on the glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) enzyme and the synap-
tic membrane protein amphiphysin. 1 Three variants of SPS have
been recognized: (i) a purely autoimmune variant that is linked
to anti-GAD antibodies and commonly associated with other auto-
immune diseases, mainly Type I diabetes mellitus and autoim-
mune thyroid disease; (ii) a less common paraneoplastic variant
related to breast cancer and small-cell lung cancer that is charac-
terized by anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies; and (iii) an idiopathic
variant that has no detectable autoantibodies. While the patho-
genic role of anti-GAD antibodies is uncertain, 2 a convincing role
of anti-amphiphysin antibodies has been established through the
passive transfer of SPS to rats.
3 These data taken together have
prompted clinicians to treat SPS with plasmapheresis, intravenous
(i.v.) immunoglobulins (Ig) or immunosuppressive agents. Treat-
ment generally slows the course of the disease or, at best, improves
muscle rigidity, but rarely achieves a total remission.
4 Rituximab,
by contrast, has shown promising results. Baker et al. ﬁrst reported
its efﬁcacy in 2005;
5 however, no subsequent publication has con-
ﬁrmed the ﬁndings.
We demonstrate the efﬁcacy of rituximab in a patient with par-
aneoplastic SPS associated with a thymoma, who secondarily
developed Type I diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroiditis,
and who produced both anti-GAD and anti-amphiphysin autoanti-
bodies. The patient’s condition initially showed a marked improve-
ment after a thymectomy followed by treatment with i.v. Ig,
prednisone, and mycophenolate mofetil (MM) but the disease re-
lapsed and the patient produced a persistent high titre of anti-
GAD and anti-amphiphysin antibodies. Following treatment with
rituximab, the patient achieved a complete remission with sup-
pression of anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies.
2. Case report
A 53-year-old caucasian man was admitted to our unit for pain-
ful muscle spasms affecting the neck, back, arms and legs and a
stiffness of the spinal column, and muscles of the abdomen and
legs. The patient was bed-bound. His muscle tone was markedly
increased in all muscle groups, predominantly in the axial and
proximal limb muscles, and his leg spasms were precipitated by
movement, startle, and light touch. The spinal column was hyper-
lordotic, and the patient was unable to walk. In a standing position,
the maximum hand–ground distance was 60 cm. Electromyogra-
phy studies demonstrated spontaneous involuntary motor unit
potentials affecting both the agonist and antagonist muscles.
Serum anti-GAD antibodies were positive and had a titre of
90 IU/mL (N < 1.5); anti-amphiphysin antibodies were also positive
and had a titre of more than 1/6400 IU/mL. The patient carried the
allele DQB1 06. Anti-Hu, Yo, RI, CV2, MA1 and MA2 antibodies
were negative. Tomodensitometry and a positron emission tomog-
raphy (PET)/CT scan showed a thymoma and a histological exami-
nation revealed it was a lympho-epithelial type. Surgical resection
was followed by treatment with prednisone, 60 mg/day, for

1 month. This was progressively reduced to 10 mg/day for
28 months, and administered with 400 mg/day of i.v. Ig for 5 days,
which was repeated monthly for 14 months. In addition, 1 g MM
was given twice daily with 20 mg/day diazepam and 30 mg/day
baclofen; the patient also underwent intensive physiotherapy.
His condition improved gradually yet he experienced resid-
ual stiffness mainly affecting the back, and muscles of the abdo-
men and limbs; however, the spasms were suppressed. The
patient was able to walk, but his gait was slow and awkward.
The anti-amphiphysin antibody titre fell to 1/1600 IU/mL, but
anti-GAD antibodies remained elevated with a titre ranging
between 70.74 IU/mL and 142.7 IU/mL. The patient developed dia-
betes mellitus 6 months after diagnosis as well as autoimmune
thyroiditis and had an anti-thyroperoxidase antibody titre of
1/800 IU/mL.
One year after a thymectomy, while the patient was still being
treated with prednisone, monthly i.v. Ig and MM, his muscle pains
and stiffness worsened and spasms reappeared in his legs. Conse-
quently, diazepam and baclofen were increased to 30 mg/day and
40 mg/day, respectively, without success. Rituximab was adminis-
tered i.v. at a dose of 350 mg/m
2 per week, for 4 weeks. After
15 days, contraction of the spinal muscles showed improvement
and the hand–ground distance was 30 cm. The abdominal stiffness
had disappeared, and the patient was able to walk a distance of
more than 500 metres, as well as stand and shower himself. Diaz-
epam and baclofen were tapered to 5 mg/day and 10 mg/day,
respectively, without relapse. The anti-amphiphysin antibody titre
fell from 1/1600 IU/mL to 1/100 IU/mL.
The patient’s symptoms began to reappear 8 months later and
he was given a single dose of rituximab. His condition improved
again after 8 days and his pain and muscle stiffness completely dis-
appeared with a total recovery of independence. Anti-amphiphysin
antibodies were no longer detectable. Twenty months after the
second administration of rituximab the patient’s condition re-
mained stable. He was able to walk and run normally, drive a
car, and was able to work. While the serum anti-amphiphysin anti-
bodies were no longer detectable, anti-GAD antibodies remained
strongly positive (Table 1). Nevertheless, his diabetes mellitus im-
proved, as conﬁrmed by a reduction of antidiabetic drugs, and no
hypothyroidism was detected during follow-up. Tomodensitome-
try was repeated every 6 months for 2 years, and was completed
by a PET/CT scan 1 year after the diagnosis, which did not show
any tumor aside from the thymoma.
3. Discussion
SPS is an autoimmune disorder, resulting from B cell-mediated
clonal production of autoantibodies against presynaptic inhibitory
epitopes on the GAD enzyme and the synaptic membrane protein
amphiphysin.
1 Two variants have been categorized according to
autoantibody types: (i) a purely autoimmune variant, characterized
by anti-GAD antibodies and involvement of the DQ B1 0201 allele,
and commonly associated with autoimmune diseases such as diabe-
tes mellitus and autoimmune thyroiditis, as well as myasthenia gra-
vis, vitiligo and celiac disease; and (ii) a paraneoplastic variant,
occurring in 10% of SPS patients, characterized by anti-amphiphysin
antibodies and commonly associated with breast cancer and small-
cell lung cancer. In our patient, the two variants were associated. The
patient had a history of thymoma, diabetes mellitus and autoim-

mune thyroiditis and his serum carried both types of autoantibodies.
The presence of a thymoma and anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies
suggested a paraneoplastic variant, but the co-occurrence of anti-
GAD diabetes mellitus and autoimmune thyroiditis suggested the
existence of an overlap syndrome. To our knowledge, the association
of both variants in the same patient has never been reported. The role
of autoantibodies in the pathogenesis of SPS is thought to be medi-
ated either by an intrathecal sensitization of autoantibody-reactive
CD4+ T cells, or a peripheral antigen sensitization followed by central
nervous system antigen recognition by autoantibodies that cross the
blood–brain barrier.

The respective roles of anti-GAD and anti-amphiphysin anti-
bodies are controversial. The role of anti-GAD is uncertain, 2 as its
presence does not correlate with the clinical symptoms, thus cast-
ing doubt on its direct pathogenic effect. SPS, for example, was not
transferred to two newborns of a patient with SPS via anti-GAD
antibodies, even after 8 years. 6 By contrast, the role of anti-amphi-
physin antibodies has been well established; transfer of human IgG
fraction to rats induced typical SPS symptoms (with a dose-depen-
dent pathogenic effect).
3 Other antigens may be relevant; for
example, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor-associated
protein, which is responsible for the stability and the surface
expression of the GABA receptor. These data suggest an autoim-
mune B cell-mediated mechanism, which is able to impair the syn-
thesis of both GAD and GABA, has a key role in the development of
SPS. This conﬁrms the rationale to treat SPS with immunosuppres-
sors, with concurrent treatment with neuromodulators including
benzodiazepines and baclofen.
Although corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, and MM have par-
tially alleviated symptoms in some patients, only i.v. Ig have in-
duced signiﬁcant improvement in a placebo-controlled crossover
trial with 16 participants. Patients in the treatment arm demon-
strated an objective improvement in functional scores associated
with a signiﬁcant reduction in anti-GAD antibodies.
7 Furthermore,
of seven patients with thymoma, six patients – including ours –
have improved following thymectomy, and a decrease of anti-
GAD antibodies was seen in three patients; however, in all patients
treated with various immunomodulator drugs the results were
incomplete. In our patient, thymectomy followed by i.v. Ig, predni-
sone, and MM induced a signiﬁcant decrease in muscle stiffness
and spasms, thus enabling the patient to walk again and perform
some daily activities, but with a residual disability impairing his
independence. Treatment did not signiﬁcantly alter the titre of
anti-GAD antibodies but the anti-amphiphysin autoantibody titre
was reduced from 1/6400 IU/mL to 1/1600 IU/mL.
Rituximab treatment, by contrast, was a very effective and was
followed by the suppression of anti-amphiphysin antibodies.
Although it is not possible to exclude a direct progressive effect
of the immunosuppressors over time, the dramatic improvement
of the muscle symptoms after rituximab treatment and the de-
crease in anti-amphiphysin autoantibodies suggest a direct effect
due to rituximab. Our ﬁndings conﬁrm the efﬁcacy of rituximab
originally demonstrated by Baker et al. in 2005.
5
4. Conclusion
Rituximab has demonstrated efﬁcacy in the treatment of
numerous autoimmune disorders, and it also has promising appli-
cations for patients with SPS. The positive correlation between the
clinical improvement of the patient and the elimination of anti-
amphiphysin antibodies provides additional evidence for the
inhibitory role of this antibody on GABAergic neurons.
